59: 
60: fn build_ui(app: &Application) {
61:     // Shared app state (mutable through Rc<RefCell> across callbacks).
62:     let demo = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Demo {
63:         engine: Engine::new(),
64:         ring: RingTransport::new(),
65:         count: 0,
66:         on_click: None,
67:     }));
68: 
69:     let window = ApplicationWindow::builder()
70:         .application(app)
71:         .title("Pathland GTK4 Demo")
72:         .default_width(420)
73:         .default_height(220)
74:         .build();
75: 
76:     let root = GtkBox::new(Orientation::Vertical, 0);
77:     window.set_child(Some(&root));
78: 
79:     // Initial render through the shared ring.
80:     let demo_ren = Rc::clone(&demo);
81:     let root_ren = root.clone();
82:     let re_render = move || render(&demo_ren, &root_ren);
83:     re_render();
84: 
85:     // Button click: apply state change, then re-render through the ring.
86:     let demo_click = Rc::clone(&demo);
87:     let root_click = root.clone();
88:     let on_click: Rc<dyn Fn()> = Rc::new(move || {
89:         let mut d = demo_click.borrow_mut();
90:         d.count = d.count.wrapping_add(1);
91:         drop(d);
92:         render(&demo_click, &root_click);
93:     });
94:     demo.borrow_mut().on_click = Some(on_click);
95: 
96:     window.present();
97: }
98: 
99: /// Pipeline: DSL -> engine -> shared ring -> RenderTree -> GTK widgets.
100: ///
101: /// The engine writes opcodes into the ring's producer view; the driver reads
102: /// the completed frame from the same ring via `FrameSource`. Zero-copy.
103: fn render(demo: &Rc<RefCell<Demo>>, root: &GtkBox) {
104:     let mut d = demo.borrow_mut();
105:     let on_click: Option<Rc<dyn Fn()>> = d.on_click.clone();
106:     let mut tree = build_tree(d.count);
107:     assign_ids(&mut tree, &mut 1);
108: 
109:     // Disjoint field borrows: engine (producer state) and ring (transport).
110:     let Demo {
111:         engine,
112:         ring,
113:         count: _,
114:         on_click: _,
115:     } = &mut *d;
116: 
117:     // 1. Producer writes opcodes into the shared ring.
118:     {
119:         let mut guest = ring.producer();
120:         guest.begin_frame();
121:         engine.emit(&tree, &mut guest).ok();
122:         guest.end_frame();
123:     }
124: 
125:     // 2. Consumer reads the completed frame from the same ring.
126:     let frame = ring.next_frame().ok().flatten().expect("a frame after emit");
127:     let frame = frame.frame();
128: 
129:     // 3. Apply the frame to the native-element description.
130:     let mut render = RenderTree::default();
131:     render.apply_frame(frame);
132: 
133:     // 4. Rebuild the GTK widget hierarchy.
134:     while let Some(child) = root.first_child() {
135:         root.remove(&child);
136:     }
137:     if let Some(root_node_id) = render.root().map(|n| n.id) {
138:         root.append(&render_node(&render, root_node_id, on_click));
139:     }
140:     root.show();
141: }
142: 
143: /// Build a GTK widget subtree for a node id from the `RenderTree`.
144: fn render_node(render: &RenderTree, id: u32, on_click: Option<Rc<dyn Fn()>>) -> gtk::Widget {
145:     let node = render.node(id).unwrap();
146:     match node.component_type {
147:         pathland_opcode::component_type::VSTACK => {
148:             let bx = GtkBox::new(Orientation::Vertical, spacing(render, id));
149:             bx.set_halign(Align::Fill);
150:             bx.set_valign(Align::Fill);
151:             for child in &node.children {
152:                 bx.append(&render_node(render, *child, on_click.clone()));
153:             }
154:             bx.upcast()
155:         }
156:         pathland_opcode::component_type::HSTACK => {
157:             let bx = GtkBox::new(Orientation::Horizontal, spacing(render, id));
158:             bx.set_halign(Align::Center);
159:             bx.set_valign(Align::Center);
160:             for child in &node.children {
161:                 bx.append(&render_node(render, *child, on_click.clone()));
162:             }
163:             bx.upcast()
164:         }
165:         pathland_opcode::component_type::TEXT => {
166:             let label = Label::new(Some(node.text.as_deref().unwrap_or("")));
167:             apply_text_style(&label, render, id);
168:             label.upcast()
169:         }
170:         pathland_opcode::component_type::BUTTON => {
171:             let btn = gtk::Button::with_label(node.text.as_deref().unwrap_or(""));
172:             if let Some(cb) = on_click {
173:                 btn.connect_clicked(move |_| cb());
174:             }
175:             btn.upcast()
176:         }
177:         _ => Label::new(Some("")).upcast(),
178:     }
179: }
180: 
181: /// Spacing property value for a node (default 4).
182: fn spacing(render: &RenderTree, id: u32) -> i32 {
183:     render
184:         .node(id)
185:         .and_then(|n| n.properties.get(&pathland_opcode::property_id::SPACING))
186:         .map(|b| f32::from_bits(*b) as i32)
187:         .unwrap_or(4)
188: }
189: 
190: /// Apply color/font-size text style from properties via Pango attributes.
191: fn apply_text_style(label: &Label, render: &RenderTree, id: u32) {
192:     let node = render.node(id).unwrap();
193:     let attrs = pango::AttrList::new();
194:     if let Some(fs) = node.properties.get(&pathland_opcode::property_id::FONT_SIZE) {
195:         // Font size is stored in points (f32); pango scales points to device units.
196:         let pts = (f32::from_bits(*fs).max(0.0) as i32) * 1000;
197:         attrs.insert(pango::AttrSize::new(pts));
198:     }
199:     if let Some(color) = node.properties.get(&pathland_opcode::property_id::COLOR) {
200:         let c = *color;
201:         let red = (((c >> 16) & 0xFF) as u16) * 257;
202:         let green = (((c >> 8) & 0xFF) as u16) * 257;
203:         let blue = ((c & 0xFF) as u16) * 257;
204:         let mut fg = pango::AttrColor::new_foreground(red, green, blue);
205:         fg.set_start_index(0);
206:         fg.set_end_index(u32::MAX);
207:         attrs.insert(fg);
208:     }
209:     label.set_attributes(Some(&attrs));
210: }

55:     /// Apply a frame's opcodes to this tree (a delta).
56:     pub fn apply_frame(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>) {
57:         for op in frame.opcodes() {

67:                     self.nodes.remove(&op.a());
68:                 }
69:                 (category::TREE, tree::INSERT_CHILD) => {
70:                     let (parent, child) = (op.a(), op.b());
71:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
72:                         if !p.children.contains(&child) {
73:                             p.children.push(child);
74:                         }
75:                     }
76:                     if let Some(c) = self.nodes.get_mut(&child) {
77:                         c.parent = Some(parent);
78:                     }
79:                 }
80:                 (category::TREE, tree::REMOVE_CHILD) => {
81:                     let (parent, child) = (op.a(), op.b());
82:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
83:                         p.children.retain(|c| *c != child);
84:                     }

Now I understand the current state:
- `pathland-gtk-demo` is a Rust binary that uses GTK APIs directly inline (render_node builds GtkBox/Label/Button). The GTK-rendering logic is coupled into the demo, not a reusable "GTK renderer".
- `pathland-host` is the RenderTree (host reader that decodes opcodes into a native-element description). This is a good abstraction already — but the GTK mapping is in the demo.
- The Java demo (`DemoApp.java`) uses Swing directly.
- `DemoHeadless.java` reads opcodes zero-copy (no rendering).

The user wants:
1. A proper GTK renderer (separate reusable component).
2. Rust demo: uses Pathland DSL, rendered via the GTK renderer (no GTK API usage in the demo).
3. Java demo: uses Pathland DSL (already does via pathland-native), rendered via the GTK renderer (no Swing, no GTK API usage in the demo).
4. No Swing anywhere.

The architecture challenge: Java can't natively create GTK widgets without GTK bindings. The GTK renderer must be native (Rust/C). So the GTK renderer lives in Rust, and the Java demo must somehow invoke it.

Let me think about the cleanest architecture given the existing `pathland-native` C-ABI shim:

Current flow for Java:
- Java DSL → Bridge → pathland_native_* C ABI → NativeHost (retained tree) → Engine → opcodes → shared ring → (Java reads ring zero-copy).

For a GTK renderer shared by both:
- The GTK renderer should be a Rust crate (`pathland-gtk`) that consumes opcode frames (from a ring/shared memory or from a decoded batch) and renders to GTK widgets, exposing a clean API that doesn't require the demo to touch GTK.
- Rust demo: builds DSL → engine → ring → GtkRenderer::render(frame) → window. The demo still needs to set up the GTK Application/window and run the main loop though. "Demos must not use gtk apis directly" — hmm, but the demo must at least start the app and run the loop. Maybe the renderer provides a `GtkRenderer::run(app_id, title, render_fn)` that handles Application creation, window, and loop, and the demo only provides the Pathland tree + a callback for events.

Actually let me re-read the user's exact words:

"Both demos must use the gtk renderer and the demos must not use gtk apis directly."

So: the GTK renderer encapsulates ALL GTK API usage. The demos call the renderer (and Pathland) only.

For Java: the GTK renderer must be callable from Java. Options:
1. The GTK renderer is part of `pathland-native` (or a new cdylib like `libpathland_gtk`), exposed via C ABI. Java loads it via JNA, drives the DSL (already), then calls `pathland_gtk_run(host, app_id, title)` which runs the GTK main loop and renders the retained tree from the host's ring. Java never touches GTK.

2. The GTK renderer is a standalone Rust process; Java launches it and communicates via shared memory/socket. More complex.

Option 1 is cleanest and aligns with the existing `pathland-native` cdylib approach. The renderer would run in-process with the JVM. GTK on macOS (darwin) with a Java JVM embedding — this requires the GTK main loop to run on the main thread, which can conflict with JVM. Actually, GTK can run in a separate thread with some care (gtk main loop in a background thread). This is the standard approach for embedding GTK in a non-C-main process.

But wait — there's a bigger architectural consideration. The user's phrasing suggests they want a "renderer for gtk" as a distinct deliverable. Let me think about what "renderer" means here in the Pathland architecture:

From AGENTS.md: "Native elements everywhere: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop". And Principle 1: "Renderers are pure functions of the opcode stream."

So a "GTK renderer" = a component that consumes opcode frames and produces/maintains GTK widgets (its rendered-output tree). The renderer owns the GTK widget tree; it applies deltas.

So the plan should be:

1. **New crate `pathland-gtk`** (or `pathland-gtk-renderer`): the GTK4 renderer.
   - Depends on `pathland-host` (RenderTree) + gtk4 crates.
   - API like:
     - `GtkRenderer::new()` — holds a `RenderTree` and a map of id → GTK widget (the rendered-output tree).
     - `renderer.apply_frame(frame)` — applies opcode deltas to GTK widgets.
     - `renderer.widget_for(id)`, `renderer.root_widget()`.
     - Maybe `GtkRenderer::run(app_id, title, producer)` that sets up Application/window/main loop and wires a FrameSource to re-render — so the demo doesn't touch GTK at all.
   - Actually, to keep the demo GTK-free, the renderer should expose a high-level `run` that takes a "frame source" / callback. But event routing (button clicks) needs to round-trip back to the app.

Let me think about how the Rust demo would look:
```rust
fn main() {
    // Build tree, assign ids, engine emits into ring...
    GtkRenderer::run(APP_ID, "Pathland Demo", |frame_source| {
        // render each frame
    });
}
```

Hmm, this is getting into design. Let me step back and identify the key architectural questions I need to ask the user, then present a plan.

Actually, let me reconsider the Java side more concretely, because that's the crux.

**How does Java render to GTK?**

The realistic options:

**Option A — GTK renderer as a Rust cdylib, embedded via JNA (in-process).**
- `pathland-gtk` becomes a `cdylib` (or `pathland-native` grows a GTK module).
- Java demo: uses Pathland DSL → `pathland_native_*` to build tree + emit → calls `pathland_gtk_run(host, ...)` which starts GTK in the current process, reads the host's ring frames, and renders. Button events routed back via a callback into Java (JNA callback).
- Pros: single GTK renderer (Rust), both demos share it. Java stays GTK-free.
- Cons: GTK-in-JVM embedding on macOS; JNA callback marshaling for events; GTK main loop threading.

**Option B — GTK renderer as a standalone Rust process; Java talks over IPC.**
- The GTK renderer is a Rust binary. Java demo drives Pathland, serializes opcodes (NetBatchEncoder), and sends to the renderer process over a socket/stdin. The renderer reads frames and renders GTK.
- Pros: clean process isolation, no GTK-in-JVM issues.
- Cons: needs IPC transport (the transport layer exists — NetBatchEncoder!). But two-way events (button clicks back to Java) need a return channel. More moving parts.

**Option C — Java uses GTK4 Java bindings directly (Java renderer).**
- Rejected: user says demos must not use GTK APIs directly, and "renderer for gtk" should be shared. Also Java GTK bindings are immature.

The most architecturally consistent with the existing code (pathland-native cdylib + JNA + zero-copy ring) is **Option A**: extend `pathland-native` (or add `pathland-gtk` as a cdylib) with a GTK renderer that Java drives via JNA.

But actually, wait. Let me reconsider. The user says "a demo in rust and a demo in java that both uses pathland. And then I want a renderer for gtk. Both demos must use the gtk renderer."

Maybe the simplest correct interpretation: 
- The GTK renderer is a Rust library (crate `pathland-gtk`).
- The Rust demo uses it directly (links the crate).
- The Java demo... needs to use GTK renderer too. Since Java can't link a Rust crate, the Java demo must go through the C ABI (pathland-native), and the GTK renderer must be exposed via that C ABI too.

So the GTK renderer needs a C ABI surface for Java. This means the GTK renderer either lives in `pathland-native` (already a cdylib) or is a separate cdylib `pathland-gtk` exposing `pathland_gtk_*` C functions.

- Java demo: Pathland DSL (via pathland-native C ABI) → renderer (no Swing, no GTK API in demo).

The crux is Java→GTK. Let me think about the two realistic approaches and present them.

**Approach 1: GTK renderer in Rust cdylib, embedded in the Java process via JNA.**
- New crate `pathland-gtk` with `crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]`, exposing:
  - Rust API: `GtkRenderer` (applies frames to GTK widget tree).
  - C ABI: `pathland_gtk_*` functions so Java can drive it.
- `pathland-native` already produces opcodes in a ring. The GTK renderer reads that ring (or the NativeHost hands frames to it).
- Java: `pathland_native_create()` → build DSL → emit → `pathland_gtk_run(host)` runs GTK main loop, reads ring frames, renders. Button click → event ingress back to Java via JNA callback → Java increments count → rebuild → emit → renderer re-renders.
- This is the most integrated approach but GTK-in-JVM has threading/main-loop concerns on macOS.

**Approach 2: GTK renderer as standalone Rust process; Java (and optionally Rust) communicate over IPC.**
- `pathland-gtk` is a binary (or library + binary harness) that reads opcode batches over a transport (NetBatchEncoder already exists) and renders GTK.
- Java demo drives Pathland, encodes frames (there's a NetBatchEncoder in Rust, but Java would need its own encode or use the native encoder), sends over a socket to the renderer process.
- Events route back over the socket to Java.
- Rust demo could either use the renderer library in-process OR also go over IPC for symmetry. But user wants "both demos use the gtk renderer" — if the Rust demo runs in-process with the renderer library and Java goes over IPC, that's asymmetric but still "uses the same renderer".

Given the existing architecture (pathland-native cdylib + zero-copy ring + JNA), and the session's emphasis on "Native (non-WASM) path: pathland-native is a cdylib ... Swift/Java/C# link it via FFI ... read opcodes zero-copy (no serialization, no WASM on desktop)", I believe **Approach 1** is the intended path: the GTK renderer is a native Rust component that Java drives via FFI, just like it drives pathland-native.

But there's a subtlety: the user says "the demos must not use gtk apis directly". For the Java demo, if it calls `pathland_gtk_run(...)` via JNA, it's not using GTK APIs directly — it's using the Pathland GTK renderer via FFI. That satisfies the requirement.

However, there's also a question about whether the renderer should be a separate crate or part of pathland-native. Given the renderer needs gtk4 deps (which are heavy and desktop-only), keeping it separate from pathland-native (which should stay lightweight and linkable on non-desktop too) is cleaner. So: new crate `pathland-gtk` (cdylib + rlib).

Let me also reconsider: is there an even simpler framing? The user might just want:
1. Extract the GTK rendering from `pathland-gtk-demo` into a `pathland-gtk` renderer crate.
2. The Rust demo (`pathland-gtk-demo`) becomes a thin driver: authors DSL, emits, calls renderer. No GTK imports in the demo's own code.
3. The Java demo drops Swing entirely and instead launches the GTK renderer. 

The Java→GTK question is unavoidable and needs clarification. Let me ask the user.

Actually, let me also consider: maybe the user wants the Java demo to ALSO drive the Rust GTK renderer through the existing pathland-native C ABI, by having pathland-native (or a new pathland-gtk cdylib) expose a `pathland_gtk_run` entry point. That's Approach 1.

Let me also think about the event/click loop for Java. Currently the Java demo increments count on button click (Swing ActionListener). With GTK renderer, the button click must route GTK→renderer→app. In the Rust demo, the renderer sets up a click callback that mutates the app state. For Java, the renderer would need to call back into Java (JNA callback) with an event (e.g., "button id=4 clicked" → which is already the EVENT category: POINTER_UP on targetId=4). Then Java handles the event, increments, rebuilds, re-emits.

Actually, the Pathland protocol has EVENT opcodes (host→guest) for raw inputs. The renderer would generate EVENT opcodes when a GTK button is clicked, and route them to the app (Java). Then Java responds by updating the tree and re-emitting. This is exactly the "renderer is dumb, app is smart" model. The renderer reports raw events; the app decides what to do.

So the event ingress path needs to exist from the renderer back to Java. In pathland-native, there's already an `input: dispatch(event)` concept in the WIT world, but for native it's not implemented (events aren't routed back yet). The session noted "host → guest events over the network transport" is deferred, and "TEXT_FIELD editing" deferred.

For the demo counter, we need at minimum: renderer detects GTK button click → calls a callback (Rust closure for the Rust demo; C function pointer for Java via JNA) → app updates count → re-emit → renderer re-renders.

1: //! Transport abstraction: how opcode batches move from producer to consumer.
2: //!
3: //! The UI runtime produces renderer-neutral opcodes and knows nothing about the
4: //! transport. This module defines the boundary between:
5: //!
6: //! - the **producer** (opcode engine) that emits opcodes, and
7: //! - the **consumer** (driver) that reads them.
8: //!
9: //! Local transports (shared-memory ring) may be zero-copy; remote transports
10: //! (WebSocket/IPC) copy and serialize. Both conform to the same traits.
11: //!
12: //! The two ends are deliberately separate because a transport is often split
13: //! across a process/IPC boundary, with different backpressure and blocking
14: //! semantics on each side.
15: 
16: use pathland_opcode::Frame;
17: 
18: /// A single in-memory transport unit: one frame of opcodes + arena plus
19: /// transport metadata. Distinct from the raw opcode stream and from the
20: /// wire-format batch.
21: pub struct OpcodeBatch<'a> {
22:     frame: Frame<'a>,
23:     /// Transport direction bitmask (see [`crate::direction`]).
24:     direction: u16,
25: }
26: 
27: impl<'a> OpcodeBatch<'a> {
28:     /// Wrap a frame as a transport batch (guest → host by default).
29:     pub fn new(frame: Frame<'a>, direction: u16) -> Self {
30:         Self { frame, direction }
31:     }
32: 
33:     /// The frame carried by this batch.
34:     pub fn frame(&self) -> &Frame<'a> {
35:         &self.frame
36:     }
37: 
38:     /// Transport direction bitmask.
39:     pub fn direction(&self) -> u16 {
40:         self.direction
41:     }
42: }
43: 
44: /// Errors produced by a transport while sending or receiving.
45: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
46: pub enum TransportError {
47:     /// The consumer has not drained; the producer should retain and retry.
48:     Backpressure,
49:     /// The transport is closed/terminated.
50:     Closed,
51:     /// The peer violated the protocol.
52:     Protocol(ProtocolError),
53: }
54: 
55: /// Sub-errors for protocol violations.
56: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
57: pub enum ProtocolError {
58:     /// The remote sent a version this side does not support.
59:     BadVersion,
60:     /// The payload is malformed (bad magic, truncated, bad length).
61:     Malformed,
62:     /// A raw input could not be interpreted.
63:     BadInput,
64: }
65: 
66: /// Handles raw-input events arriving from the host (renderer → engine).
67: ///
68: /// The driver resolves a raw input to a node id (via hit-testing) and dispatches
69: /// it here; the transport's guest side forwards it to the guest engine.
70: pub trait InputSink {
71:     /// Deliver a raw input (host → guest).
72:     fn dispatch(&mut self, event: &pathland_opcode::Event);
73: }
74: 
75: /// The consumer side of a transport: the driver reads frames here.
76: ///
77: /// A transport may be blocking or non-blocking; `next_frame` reflects that.
78: /// The returned `Frame` borrows the transport's backing memory (zero-copy when
79: /// possible); consume it before the next call.
80: pub trait FrameSource {
81:     /// Read the next available frame, or `None` if none is ready.
82:     ///
83:     /// Blocking vs non-blocking semantics are transport-specific (documented
84:     /// per implementation).
85:     fn next_frame(&mut self) -> Result<Option<OpcodeBatch<'_>>, TransportError>;
86: }
87: 
88: /// A consumer-side transport that can also send raw inputs back to the guest.
89: pub trait DriverTransport: FrameSource {
90:     /// Send a raw input from the host to the guest over this transport.
91:     fn send_input(&mut self, event: &pathland_opcode::Event) -> Result<(), TransportError>;
92: }

1: //! Shared-memory ring transport (zero-copy, SPSC).
2: //!
3: //! The producer (opcode engine) and consumer (native driver) share one linear
4: //! memory buffer containing the ring + arena. The producer writes 16-byte
5: //! opcodes via `pathland_opcode::Guest`; the consumer reads completed frames via
6: //! `pathland_opcode::Host`. No copying, no batching, no serialization — this is
7: //! the high-performance local path.
8: 
9: use pathland_opcode::{init_memory, Guest, Host, MemoryLayout};
10: 
11: use crate::traits::{DriverTransport, FrameSource, OpcodeBatch, TransportError};
12: 
13: /// A zero-copy SPSC shared-memory ring transport.
14: ///
15: /// Owns the linear-memory buffer (header + ring + arena). Producers and
16: /// consumers are granted short-lived `Guest`/`Host` views over the same buffer
17: /// via the borrowed methods, so opcodes flow in place with no copies.
18: #[derive(Debug)]
19: pub struct RingTransport {
20:     /// Shared linear memory (header | ring | arena).
21:     mem: Vec<u8>,
22:     /// Ring/arena geometry.
23:     layout: MemoryLayout,
24: }
25: 
26: impl RingTransport {
27:     /// Create a ring transport with a default layout and a zeroed header.
28:     pub fn new() -> Self {
29:         let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
30:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
31:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
32:         Self { mem, layout }
33:     }
34: 
35:     /// Create a ring transport over a caller-provided buffer/layout.
36:     pub fn with_buffer(mem: Vec<u8>, layout: MemoryLayout) -> Self {
37:         Self { mem, layout }
38:     }
39: 
40:     /// The memory layout (region geometry).
41:     pub fn layout(&self) -> &MemoryLayout {
42:         &self.layout
43:     }
44: 
45:     /// Create a producer view over the shared buffer (writes opcodes + arena).
46:     ///
47:     /// Drop the returned `Guest` before calling `next_frame`; producer and
48:     /// consumer must not overlap borrows.
49:     pub fn producer(&mut self) -> Guest<'_> {
50:         Guest::new(&mut self.mem, &self.layout)
51:     }
52: 
53:     /// Peak at the raw underlying buffer (for embedding/custom transports).
54:     pub fn buffer(&self) -> &[u8] {
55:         &self.mem
56:     }
57: }
58: 
59: impl Default for RingTransport {
60:     fn default() -> Self {
61:         Self::new()
62:     }
63: }
64: 
65: impl FrameSource for RingTransport {
66:     fn next_frame(&mut self) -> Result<Option<OpcodeBatch<'_>>, TransportError> {
67:         let mut host = Host::new(&mut self.mem, &self.layout);
68:         let mut frames = host.frames();
69:         match frames.pop() {
70:             Some(frame) => Ok(Some(OpcodeBatch::new(
71:                 frame,
72:                 crate::direction::GUEST_TO_HOST,
73:             ))),
74:             None => Ok(None),
75:         }
76:     }
77: }
78: 
79: impl DriverTransport for RingTransport {
80:     fn send_input(&mut self, event: &pathland_opcode::Event) -> Result<(), TransportError> {
81:         // Events cross the boundary as EVENT-category opcodes in the ring. The
82:         // host writes them at the producer side of the shared transport; a full
83:         // host → guest ring is reserved for a later phase. For now route through
84:         // the guest input path (in-process call).
85:         let _ = event;
86:         Err(TransportError::Protocol(
87:             crate::ProtocolError::BadInput,
88:         ))
89:     }
90: }
91: 
92: #[cfg(test)]
93: mod tests {
94:     use super::*;
95:     use pathland_opcode::{category, property_id, tree};
96: 
97:     #[test]
98:     fn ring_round_trips_frames() {
99:         let mut ring = RingTransport::new();
100:         // Producer writes opcodes into the shared buffer via Guest.
101:         {
102:             let mut guest = ring.producer();
103:             guest.begin_frame();
104:             guest.create_node(1, 0x0002).unwrap();
105:             guest.create_node(2, 0x0003).unwrap();
106:             guest.insert_child(1, 2, 0).unwrap();
107:             guest
108:                 .set_property(2, property_id::SPACING, 0x04, 4.0f32.to_bits())
109:                 .unwrap();
110:             guest.end_frame();
111:         }
112:         // Consumer reads the frame back from the same shared buffer.
113:         let batch = ring.next_frame().unwrap().expect("a frame");
114:         let ops: Vec<_> = batch.frame().opcodes().collect();
115:         assert_eq!(ops.len(), 4);
116:         assert_eq!(ops[0].category(), category::TREE);
117:         assert!(ops.iter().any(|o| o.command() == tree::CREATE_NODE));
118:     }
119: 
120:     #[test]
121:     fn ring_empty_when_no_frame() {
122:         let mut ring = RingTransport::new();
123:         assert!(ring.next_frame().unwrap().is_none());
124:     }
125: }

17: /// Append `op` to the ring at `writeCursor` and advance the cursor.
18: ///

299:     /// Construct a frame view over contiguous 16-byte opcode slots plus an
300:     /// arena region (`start`/`end` are byte offsets into `slots`).
301:     ///
302:     /// Used by transport backends to produce `Frame` views over their own
303:     /// buffers; `Host` builds these internally from the ring.
304:     pub fn from_parts(slots: &'a [u8], arena: &'a [u8], start: usize, end: usize) -> Self {
305:         Self {
306:             slots,
307:             arena,
308:             start,
309:             end,
310:         }
311:     }
312: 
313:     /// Iterate the opcodes in this frame, in order.
314:     pub fn opcodes(&self) -> FrameIter<'a> {
315:         FrameIter {
316:             slots: self.slots,
317:             cursor: self.start,
318:             end: self.end,
319:         }
320:     }
321: 
322:     /// Number of opcodes in the frame.
323:     pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
324:         (self.end - self.start) / Opcode::SIZE
325:     }
326: 
327:     pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
328:         self.len() == 0
329:     }
330: 
331:     /// Read an arena entry by offset (see `Guest::alloc` / `Guest::alloc_str`).
332:     pub fn arena_get(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a [u8], ArenaError> {
333:         arena_fn::get(self.arena, offset)
334:     }
335: 
336:     /// Read an arena string by offset.
337:     pub fn arena_str(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a str, ArenaError> {
338:         arena_fn::get_str(self.arena, offset)
339:     }
340: 
341:     /// The full arena region (for transport serialization of arena deltas).
342:     pub fn arena(&self) -> &'a [u8] {
343:         self.arena
344:     }
345: }
346: 
347: /// Iterator over the opcodes in a `Frame`.
348: pub struct FrameIter<'a> {
349:     slots: &'a [u8],
350:     cursor: usize,
351:     end: usize,
352: }
353: 
354: impl<'a> Iterator for FrameIter<'a> {
355:     type Item = Opcode;
356: 
357:     fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Opcode> {
358:         if self.cursor >= self.end {
359:             return None;
360:         }
361:         let bytes: [u8; 16] = self.slots[self.cursor..self.cursor + 16].try_into().unwrap();
362:         self.cursor += 16;
363:         Some(Opcode::from_bytes(&bytes))
364:     }
365: }
366: 
367: /// Consumer side: the host renderer reading completed frames.
368: ///
369: /// SPSC contract: the host never reads past the producer's published
370: /// `writeCursor`, and the producer never overwrites an unconsumed `readCursor`.
371: /// If the host is slow, multiple produced frames are coalesced into one `Frame`
372: /// (opcodes remain in order); the `frameCount` simply signals "new data".
373: pub struct Host<'a> {
374:     header: &'a mut [u8],
375:     slots: &'a [u8],
376:     arena: &'a [u8],
377:     /// Number of frames already consumed by this host view.
378:     consumed: u32,
379: }
380: 
381: impl<'a> Host<'a> {
382:     /// Create a host view over the linear memory.
383:     pub fn new(mem: &'a mut [u8], layout: &MemoryLayout) -> Self {
384:         let (header, rest) = mem.split_at_mut(memory::HEADER_SIZE);
385:         let (slots, arena) = rest.split_at_mut(layout.ring_bytes());
386:         Self {
387:             header,
388:             slots,
389:             arena,
390:             consumed: 0,
391:         }
392:     }
393: 
394:     /// Total frames produced by the guest (for diagnostics).
395:     pub fn frame_count(&self) -> u32 {
396:         header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT)
397:     }
398: 
399:     /// Consume all frames produced since the last call, advancing `readCursor`.
400:     ///
401:     /// Returns at most one `Frame` (all new opcodes since the last drain). If
402:     /// the producer produced multiple frames before this call they coalesce.
403:     pub fn frames(&mut self) -> Vec<Frame<'a>> {
404:         let frame_count = header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT);
405:         if self.consumed >= frame_count {
406:             return Vec::new();
407:         }
408:         let mask = slot_mask(self.header);
409:         let start = ring_fn::cursor(self.header, OFF_READ_CURSOR, mask);
410:         let end = ring_fn::cursor(self.header, OFF_WRITE_CURSOR, mask);
411: 
412:         // The POC producer flushes before the ring fills, so `end >= start`
413:         // always holds. Guard against a wrapped ring by draining nothing; a
414:         // wrapped producer must flush first (see OPCODE.md backpressure).
415:         if end < start {
416:             return Vec::new();
417:         }
418: 
419:         let frames = vec![Frame {
420:             slots: self.slots,
421:             arena: self.arena,
422:             start: start * Opcode::SIZE,
423:             end: end * Opcode::SIZE,
424:         }];
425: 
426:         header::set_u32(self.header, OFF_READ_CURSOR, end as u32);
427:         self.consumed = frame_count;
428:         frames
429:     }
430: }
431:

433: mod tests {
434:     use super::*;
435:     use crate::constants::{category, component_type, property_id, value_type};
436:     use alloc::vec;
437: 
438:     #[test]
439:     fn guest_host_round_trip() {
440:         let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
441:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
442:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
443: 
444:         let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
445:         guest.begin_frame();
446:         guest.create_node(1, component_type::VSTACK).unwrap();
447:         guest.insert_child(0, 1, APPEND).unwrap();
448:         guest.set_property(1, property_id::SPACING, value_type::F32, 4.0f32.to_bits()).unwrap();
449:         guest
450:             .set_property(1, property_id::PADDING, value_type::F32, 8.0f32.to_bits())
451:             .unwrap();
452:         let arena_ref = guest.set_text(1, "Hello").unwrap();
453:         assert_eq!(guest.pending(), 5);
454:         guest.end_frame();
455:         assert_eq!(guest.frame_count(), 1);
456: 
457:         let mut host = Host::new(&mut mem, &layout);
458:         assert_eq!(host.frame_count(), 1);
459:         let frames = host.frames();
460:         assert_eq!(frames.len(), 1);
461:         let frame = &frames[0];
462:         let ops: Vec<Opcode> = frame.opcodes().collect();
463:         assert_eq!(ops.len(), 5);
464:         assert_eq!(ops[0].category(), category::TREE);
465:         assert_eq!(ops[0].a(), 1);
466:         assert_eq!(ops[1].a(), 0); // parent root
467:         assert_eq!(ops[2].b() as u16, property_id::SPACING);
468:         assert_eq!(ops[2].c_f32(), 4.0);
469:         assert_eq!(frame.arena_str(arena_ref).unwrap(), "Hello");
470:         // Second drain is empty.
471:         assert!(host.frames().is_empty());
472:     }
473:

475:     fn ring_full_is_reported() {
476:         let mut layout = MemoryLayout::default();
477:         layout.slot_count = 4; // tiny ring
478:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
479:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);

481:         let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
482:         // 4 slots -> capacity is slot_count-1 = 3 opcodes before full.

204: 
205: ## Linear Memory Layout
206: 
207: The guest engine and host share a **single linear memory**. Regions are fixed at module start:
208: 
209: ```
210: +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
211: | 0x0000  Header block (64 B)  — cursors, frame counter, layout  |
212: | 0x0040  Ring buffer (16 B × slotCount)                         |
213: | ...      (slots densely packed, 64-byte aligned base)          |
214: | 0x10040 Arena (bump region for strings / token paths / lists)  |
215: | ...                                                            |
216: +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
217: ```
218: 
219: ### Header block (64 bytes)
220: 
221: | Offset | Size | Field | Producer | Description |
222: |--------|------|-------|----------|-------------|
223: | 0x00 | 4 | `magic` | — | `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`) |
224: | 0x04 | 2 | `version` | — | Wire protocol version (1) |
225: | 0x06 | 4 | `ringOffset` | — | Byte offset of the ring region |
226: | 0x0A | 4 | `ringBytes` | — | Byte length of the ring region |
227: | 0x0E | 4 | `slotCount` | — | Number of ring slots (power of two) |
228: | 0x12 | 4 | `arenaOffset` | — | Byte offset of the arena region |
229: | 0x16 | 4 | `arenaBytes` | — | Byte length of the arena region |
230: | 0x1A | 4 | `arenaCursor` | guest | Next free byte in the arena |
231: | 0x1E | 4 | `readCursor` | host | Ring slot the host has consumed up to |
232: | 0x22 | 4 | `writeCursor` | guest | Ring slot the guest has written up to |
233: | 0x26 | 4 | `frameCount` | guest | Monotonic completed-frame counter |
234: | 0x2A | 22 | reserved | — | Zero |
235: 
236: ### Ring buffer
237: 
238: - Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
239: - **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
240: - **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
241: - **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
242: - **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.
243: 
244: ### Arena
245: 
246: - A pre-allocated **bump region** for variable-length data (strings, token paths).
247: - Every arena entry is **self-describing**: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`.
248: - Opcodes reference entries by their **byte offset** (`arenaRef`), so an entry's length is read directly from the arena — all opcodes stay 16 bytes.
249: - The guest advances `arenaCursor` monotonically (no free-list, no fragmentation). The arena MAY be reset via `META::RESET`.
250: 
251: ---
252: 
253: ## Colors
254: 
255: Literal colors are **sRGB** (IEC 61966-2-1, D65 white point), packed as `0xAARRGGBB`:
256: 
257: - `AA`: alpha (0x00 transparent – 0xFF opaque)
258: - `RR`: red, `GG`: green, `BB`: blue
259: 
260: Stored little-endian in a `u32` payload. Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation remain **renderer-owned** (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)).
261: 
262: ---
263: 
264: ## Design Token System
265: 
266: ### Core Principle
267: 
268: > **The renderer owns the defaults. The application owns the overrides.**
269: 
270: This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency when the application overrides tokens.
271: 
272: ### Responsibilities
273: 
274: | Aspect | Owner | Responsibility |
275: |--------|-------|----------------|
276: | **Default Token Values** | Renderer | Define platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens |
277: | **Token Overrides** | Application | Specify overrides for cross-platform consistency |
278: | **Token Resolution** | Renderer | Resolve final token values (override or default) |
279: | **Platform Adaptation** | Renderer | Adapt default token values to platform conventions |
280: 
281: ### Token Identification
282: 
283: Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`, `font.body`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.
284: 
285: ### Token Resolution Algorithm
286: 
287: ```
288: FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath: string) -> PropertyValue:
289:     IF applicationOverrides.has(tokenPath):
290:         RETURN applicationOverrides[tokenPath]
291:     ELSE IF rendererDefaults.has(tokenPath):
292:         RETURN rendererDefaults[tokenPath]
293:     ELSE IF hasParentToken(tokenPath):
294:         RETURN resolveToken(getParentPath(tokenPath))
295:     ELSE:
296:         RETURN getFallbackValue(tokenPath)
297: ```
298: 
299: ### Renderer Responsibilities

---

## Linear Memory Layout

The guest engine and host share a **single linear memory**. Regions are fixed at module start:

```
+───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
| 0x0000  Header block (64 B)  — cursors, frame counter, layout  |
| 0x0040  Ring buffer (16 B × slotCount)                         |
| ...      (slots densely packed, 64-byte aligned base)          |
| 0x10040 Arena (bump region for strings / token paths / lists)  |
| ...                                                            |
+───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
```

### Header block (64 bytes)

| Offset | Size | Field | Producer | Description |
|--------|------|-------|----------|-------------|
| 0x00 | 4 | `magic` | — | `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`) |
| 0x04 | 2 | `version` | — | Wire protocol version (1) |
| 0x06 | 4 | `ringOffset` | — | Byte offset of the ring region |
| 0x0A | 4 | `ringBytes` | — | Byte length of the ring region |
| 0x0E | 4 | `slotCount` | — | Number of ring slots (power of two) |
| 0x12 | 4 | `arenaOffset` | — | Byte offset of the arena region |
| 0x16 | 4 | `arenaBytes` | — | Byte length of the arena region |
| 0x1A | 4 | `arenaCursor` | guest | Next free byte in the arena |
| 0x1E | 4 | `readCursor` | host | Ring slot the host has consumed up to |
| 0x22 | 4 | `writeCursor` | guest | Ring slot the guest has written up to |
| 0x26 | 4 | `frameCount` | guest | Monotonic completed-frame counter |
| 0x2A | 22 | reserved | — | Zero |

### Ring buffer

- Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
- **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
- **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
- **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
- **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.

### Arena

- A pre-allocated **bump region** for variable-length data (strings, token paths).
- Every arena entry is **self-describing**: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`.
- Opcodes reference entries by their **byte offset** (`arenaRef`), so an entry's length is read directly from the arena — all opcodes stay 16 bytes.
- The guest advances `arenaCursor` monotonically (no free-list, no fragmentation). The arena MAY be reset via `META::RESET`.

---

## Colors

Literal colors are **sRGB** (IEC 61966-2-1, D65 white point), packed as `0xAARRGGBB`:

- `AA`: alpha (0x00 transparent – 0xFF opaque)
- `RR`: red, `GG`: green, `BB`: blue

Stored little-endian in a `u32` payload. Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation remain **renderer-owned** (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)).

---

## Design Token System

### Core Principle

> **The renderer owns the defaults. The application owns the overrides.**

This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency when the application overrides tokens.

### Responsibilities

| Aspect | Owner | Responsibility |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **Default Token Values** | Renderer | Define platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens |
| **Token Overrides** | Application | Specify overrides for cross-platform consistency |
| **Token Resolution** | Renderer | Resolve final token values (override or default) |
| **Platform Adaptation** | Renderer | Adapt default token values to platform conventions |

### Token Identification

Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`, `font.body`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.

### Token Resolution Algorithm

```
FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath: string) -> PropertyValue:
    IF applicationOverrides.has(tokenPath):
        RETURN applicationOverrides[tokenPath]
    ELSE IF rendererDefaults.has(tokenPath):
        RETURN rendererDefaults[tokenPath]
    ELSE IF hasParentToken(tokenPath):
        RETURN resolveToken(getParentPath(tokenPath))
    ELSE:
        RETURN getFallbackValue(tokenPath)
```

### Renderer Responsibilities

The renderer MUST:

1. Provide platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens (e.g. `color.primary`, `font.body.size`, `space.md`).
2. Accept `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides.
3. Resolve design-token references in properties.
4. Fall back to defaults when no override exists.
5. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.

The application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` and reference tokens via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type; it MUST NOT assume specific default token values.

### Standard Token Catalog

Required core tokens (renderer MUST support with platform-appropriate defaults): `color.primary`, `color.secondary`, `color.background`, `color.surface`, `color.text.primary`, `color.text.secondary`, `color.border`, `font.body.size`, `font.body.weight`, `font.body.family`, `space.xs`–`space.lg`.

Recommended extended tokens: `color.success`, `color.warning`, `color.danger`, `color.info`, `font.heading.1`–`font.heading.6`, `font.size.heading.1`–`6`, `radius.sm`/`md`, `elevation.low`/`high`, `opacity.disabled`.

---

## Frame Lifecycle

A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:

1. Guest begins a frame.
2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.

Because the ring and arena are plain memory, the guest publishes via a single release store of `frameCount`; the host acquires on read.

Now I have a complete picture of the memory layout and event model. Key facts:

1. The header has `0x2A` reserved (22 bytes) — room to add event-ring fields.
2. The ring is single-direction (guest→host). There is NO host→guest ring.
3. Events (`Event` enum) encode to 16-byte EVENT opcodes (`Event::encode()`), and decode via `Event::try_from`.
4. `InputSink::dispatch(&Event)` is the guest-side ingress, but `RingTransport::send_input` is stubbed (`BadInput`).

So to make events "emitted via the opcode engine", I need to add a **host→guest event channel** to the shared memory: a second ring (event ring) with its own cursors (host writes, guest reads), plus header fields for it.

The reserved header space (0x2A..0x40 = 22 bytes) can hold:
- eventRingOffset (4B)
- eventRingBytes (4B) — or reuse slotCount
- eventSlotCount (4B)
- eventReadCursor (4B, guest-owned)
- eventWriteCursor (4B, host-owned)
- eventFrameCount (4B) — optional

That's ~24 bytes if I add all six; 22 bytes reserved. Tight. I can trim: reuse `slotCount` for the event ring (same slot count), and store eventRingOffset/eventRingBytes/eventReadCursor/eventWriteCursor/eventFrameCount = 20 bytes. That fits in 22.

Actually, let me think about whether I even need a full second ring for the demo, or whether there's a cleaner design.

The event flow in the counter demo:
1. GTK renderer (host) detects button click → encodes `Event::PointerUp{target, ...}` → writes EVENT opcode into event ring.
2. Guest (app) drains event ring → decodes → dispatches to on_event → increments count → re-emits TREE/STYLE into the guest→host ring.
3. Renderer's idle pump drains guest→host ring → applies delta (incremental) → updates label.

This is a clean bidirectional protocol. It's the "both directions binary" principle realized.

However, this is a substantial addition. Let me consider whether the user wants the FULL protocol event ring now, or whether they'd accept a simpler realization where events are opcode-encoded but delivered in-process via the InputSink (still "via the opcode engine" in the sense that Event::encode/try_from are used and the engine's input path ingests them).

Actually, re-reading the user: "are they emitted via the opcode engine? They should be." — The emphasis is that events go through the opcode engine (the ring/opcode stream), not a typed callback. The cleanest and most protocol-faithful is a host→guest event ring.

But wait — there's a subtlety about the WASM/WIT path. The WIT `input.dispatch(event)` is typed (WIT `event` variant), and the WASM guest's `InputGuest::dispatch` calls `app::on_event` directly. There's no event ring in the WASM path. The session context describes events as typed raw-input encode/decode with conformance vectors (the EVENT opcode bytes). So the opcode EVENT encoding exists for the wire/transport, but the in-process WASM path uses typed dispatch.

For the native path, the analogous "typed dispatch" would be `InputSink::dispatch(&Event)`. But the user wants opcode-based.

Hmm, let me reconcile. There are two layers:
1. **Protocol/wire layer**: events are EVENT opcodes (16 bytes) — for transport across a boundary.
2. **In-process dispatch layer**: typed `Event` enum dispatched to the app.

The user wants events "emitted via the opcode engine" — i.e., the renderer produces EVENT opcodes, which go through the ring (the opcode engine's shared memory), and the app/engine consumes them.

Given both demos are in-process (guest+host same process), the event ring is the natural home for this. And it aligns with the transport's `DriverTransport::send_input` (host writes input, guest reads) — currently stubbed precisely because the host→guest ring isn't implemented yet.

So the plan should implement the host→guest event ring. This is a meaningful chunk, and I should call it out clearly, including:
- Header extension (event ring geometry + cursors in the reserved 22 bytes).
- Memory layout: header | ring (guest→host) | event ring (host→guest) | arena.
- `pathland-opcode`: add `HostWriter` (writes EVENT opcodes into event ring) and `GuestReader` (reads EVENT opcodes). Or generalize the existing `Guest`/`Host` into direction-aware producers/consumers.
- `pathland-transport`: implement `RingTransport::send_input` to write EVENT opcodes into the event ring; add an event-drain method for the guest side.
- `pathland-native`: expose event writing (for the GTK renderer) and event draining (for Java to poll).
- `pathland-gtk`: renderer writes EVENT opcodes on button click.
- Demos: app drains events and dispatches.

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider the topology once more for the two demos, because "who writes events" and "who reads events" differs:

**Rust demo** (single process, all Rust):
- Guest side: `Engine` + `RingTransport` (the demo's code).
- Host side: `GtkRenderer` (in `pathland-gtk`).
- Event: GTK renderer writes EVENT opcode → event ring → demo's event loop drains → handles → re-emits.

But the demo's "event loop" — where does it drain? In the current GTK demo, the render runs inside GTK's main loop (gtk::Application::run). If the renderer runs the GTK main loop, the demo can't simultaneously run its own drain loop on the same thread. So the event drain must happen either:
- Inside the renderer's idle callback (the renderer drains the guest→host ring AND the host→guest event ring, and for events it calls into the app's handler).
- Or the app's handler is invoked by the renderer when it drains an event.

So the renderer's frame-pump (glib idle) does:
1. Drain guest→host ring → apply_frame (render).
2. Drain host→guest event ring → for each EVENT opcode, decode `Event` → call `on_event(&Event)` (the app's handler).
3. The app's handler (Rust closure / Java callback) updates state and re-emits guest→host opcodes.

This is clean! The renderer is the pump for both directions. The app just provides `on_event` + re-emit logic.

But then, is "on_event" a typed callback or opcode-based? The events flow as opcodes through the ring (opcode engine), and the renderer decodes them (Event::try_from) before handing the typed `Event` to the app. This is exactly "emitted via the opcode engine" — the renderer's button-click → EVENT opcode → ring → decoded → dispatched.

For the Java demo:
- The GTK renderer (cdylib) is in-process. It writes EVENT opcodes into the event ring (part of the NativeHost's shared memory), drains them in its idle pump, and needs to notify Java. The "on_event" for Java is a JNA callback (typed: `void onEvent(int targetId, int kind, float x, float y)` or a simpler `void onEvent(int targetId)` for the demo).

Wait, but if the renderer decodes the EVENT opcode and calls Java via JNA, then the Java side receives a typed callback. Is that "via the opcode engine"? Yes — the opcode went through the ring, was encoded/decoded by the opcode engine; the final dispatch to the app is necessarily a typed call (in Rust it's a closure, in Java it's a JNA callback). The point is the renderer→app path uses EVENT opcodes through the ring, not a bespoke side-channel.

Alternatively, for Java, the event could stay as opcodes all the way to Java: Java drains the event ring itself (via `pathland_native_drain_events` returning raw opcode bytes or decoded events) and decodes them in Java (RingReader already parses opcodes). But that duplicates decode logic in Java. Simpler: the renderer decodes and calls a JNA callback with the typed event.

Hmm, but there's a subtlety: if the renderer decodes and dispatches, then for the Rust demo the "opcode engine" is only used as a transport ring between renderer-produce and renderer-consume (same component), which is a bit circular. Let me think about who OWNS the event ring write/read.

Cleaner separation:
- **Renderer writes EVENT opcodes** into the event ring (it's the "host" producer of events).
- **App/guest reads EVENT opcodes** from the event ring (the "guest" consumer of events), decodes them, and reacts.

For the Rust demo: the demo's app logic (guest side) should read events. But the demo's guest logic runs on the GTK main thread (inside the renderer's run loop). So the demo needs a hook: the renderer's idle pump calls a guest-provided "drain events" function. 

This is essentially: `GtkRenderer::run(source, input_source, on_event)` where:
- `source` = guest→host frame source (the demo's ring).
- `input_source` = host→guest event source (the same ring's event side, or a separate event channel).
- `on_event` = app handler.

Actually, I think the cleanest design that's honest about the opcode engine:

The **event ring is part of the shared memory**, written by the renderer (host) and read by the guest (app). The `RingTransport` (or a new `BidirectionalRingTransport`) owns BOTH rings. The renderer:
- reads guest→host ring (frames) to render,
- writes host→guest event ring on user interaction.

The guest (demo/app):
- writes guest→host ring (emit),
- reads host→guest event ring (drain events → dispatch to on_event).

The GTK main loop drives both. The demo registers an `on_event` closure; the renderer's idle pump drains the event ring and invokes it.

OK, this is a solid design. It's a fair amount of work, but it's the correct, protocol-faithful approach the user is asking for.

Let me now also double-check: is there already a notion of "direction" in the transport? Yes — `crate::direction::GUEST_TO_HOST` (seen in ring.rs `OpcodeBatch::new(frame, crate::direction::GUEST_TO_HOST)`). Let me note that events would be `HOST_TO_GUEST`.

Now, scope assessment. This is a large plan:
1. `pathland-opcode`: memory layout + header extension (event ring), new writer/reader for event direction, tests, spec + conformance updates.
2. `pathland-transport`: `RingTransport` becomes bidirectional (event ring), implement `send_input`, add guest-side event drain.
3. `pathland-native`: expose event drain/write via C ABI for Java.
4. `pathland-gtk` (new): incremental renderer + event emission.
5. Demos: Rust + Java, no GTK/Swing in demo code.
6. Docs.

I need to present this comprehensively. Let me also decide on the event ring layout details for the plan.

Header extension plan (fits in reserved 22 bytes, 0x2A–0x40):
- 0x2A | 4 | `eventRingOffset` | — | Byte offset of the host→guest event ring region
- 0x2E | 4 | `eventRingBytes` | — | Byte length of the event ring region
- 0x32 | 4 | `eventSlotCount` | — | Event ring slot count (power of two)  [or reuse slotCount]
- 0x36 | 4 | `eventReadCursor` | guest | Event ring slot the guest has consumed up to
- 0x3A | 4 | `eventWriteCursor` | host | Event ring slot the host has written up to
- 0x3E | 2 | reserved | — | (2 bytes left)

That's exactly 22 bytes (0x2A..0x40). 0x2A + 4*5 = 0x3E, then 0x3E..0x40 = 2 bytes reserved. 

Memory layout becomes: header (64B) | ring (guest→host, slotCount×16) | eventRing (host→guest, eventSlotCount×16) | arena.

This changes the arena offset (moves after the event ring). `total_bytes` and `arena_offset` computations must be updated. This also affects the Java `RingReader` header offsets? The RingReader reads ring offset/slotCount/arena offset/cursors from the header — if I add a second ring and move the arena, the `OFF_ARENA_OFFSET` value changes (computed), but the field offsets (OFF_ARENA_OFFSET = 0x12) stay the same; only the VALUE changes. I'll propose a dedicated (smaller) event ring with its own slot count field in `MemoryLayout`, but note reusing slot_count is an acceptable simplification. Actually, to keep the wire format and MemoryLayout clean, I'll propose adding `event_slot_count` to `MemoryLayout` and the header.

Hmm, but adding `event_slot_count` changes `MemoryLayout` struct (used in many places, including the WASM guest and conformance). Let me keep it minimal but correct: add event ring to layout.

Actually — I realize I should be careful about scope creep and present this clearly, letting the user see the full picture. The user explicitly wants events through the opcode engine, so the event ring is in scope. But I should present it as a distinct, clearly-scoped phase and confirm.

Let me also reconsider: is there a simpler "opcode engine" event path that avoids a second ring? 

Alternative: Events go through the SAME guest→host ring? No — that's the wrong direction.

Alternative: A single bidirectional ring where the header tracks two pairs of cursors? That's basically the two-ring design sharing one slot array. Could do: one slot array, split into two halves (guest→host half + host→guest half). That's equivalent to two rings but in one contiguous region. The header would track two cursor pairs. Same complexity.

- The GTK renderer (cdylib, in-process) writes EVENT opcodes into the event ring.

For the Rust demo, the renderer reads the event ring and calls the Rust `on_event` closure.

So the renderer writes AND the renderer reads (in its idle pump) to dispatch to the app? That's a bit self-contained, but it's actually fine because the ring provides the queuing/ordering and the opcode encoding/decoding is the "protocol" boundary.

Actually, let me reconsider who writes events. In a real system:
- The renderer (host) owns the GTK widgets and detects clicks.
- The renderer writes EVENT opcodes (host→guest) into the event ring.
- The guest (app/engine) reads the event ring and dispatches.

- `FrameSource::next_frame` — guest→host frames (renderer reads). ✓ already implemented by RingTransport.
- `DriverTransport::send_input(&Event)` — host→guest events (renderer writes). Currently stubbed → implement to write EVENT opcode into event ring.
- `InputSink::dispatch(&Event)` — guest-side event ingress (app receives). Need a "drain events" method on the guest side of the ring.

- `RingTransport` gains an event ring; `send_input` writes `Event::encode()` into it; a new method (e.g., `drain_events(&mut self) -> Vec<Event>`) reads and decodes.
- A trait for the guest-side event read, or just a method on RingTransport.

- `GtkRenderer` is the HOST (renderer). It:
  - Reads guest→host frames: needs a `FrameSource`.
  - Writes host→guest events: needs `send_input` (DriverTransport).
- The APP (guest) is external (Rust closure / Java). It:

The design doesn't HARD-depend on 64-byte lines for correctness, only for the "4 per line" performance claim. That's fine — still dense, still aligned.

**1. Fixed-width types, language-guaranteed sizes.** The opcode is `u8 | u8 | u16 | u32 | u32 | u32`. In Rust, `u8`/`u16`/`u32` are *always* 1/2/4 bytes on every target — RISC-V (rv64 / RV A23), ESP32 (Xtensa and RISC-V), ARM64 (Apple M), x86, AMD. `f32` is always IEEE-754 binary32. Nothing here is `usize`, pointer-sized, or C `int`-sized, which is what would vary per platform.

**2. `#[repr(C, packed)]` guarantees exactly 16 bytes, no padding.** There's a test `size_is_16_bytes` asserting `size_of::<Opcode>() == 16`. Packed repr eliminates any compiler-inserted alignment padding, so the size is identical across every ABI.

 # Pathland Conformance Test Vectors
 
 **Wire protocol version:** 1
 **Encoding:** little-endian
 **Opcode size:** 16 bytes
 
 This document provides **golden byte arrays** for the Pathland opcode protocol (see [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)). A conforming implementation MUST:
 
 - encode each opcode to exactly these 16 bytes, and
 - decode these bytes to the equivalent opcode.
 
 The vectors are enforced by the reference Rust encoder (`pathland-opcode`,
 `crates/pathland-opcode/src/conformance.rs`).
 
 ## Opcode Layout
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 All multi-byte fields little-endian. `A`/`B`/`C` may carry `f32` bit patterns.
 
 ## Vectors
 
 ### 1. TREE:CREATE_NODE (id=1, VSTACK=0x0002)
 
 ```
 01 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
 ```
 
 - `01` category = TREE
 - `01` command = CREATE_NODE
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `01 00 00 00` A = nodeId = 1
 - `02 00 00 00` B = componentType = 0x0002 (VSTACK)
 - `00 00 00 00` C = 0
 
 ### 2. TREE:INSERT_CHILD (parent=0, child=1, index=APPEND)
 
 ```
 01 03 00 00 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 FF FF FF FF
 ```
 
 - `01` category = TREE
 - `03` command = INSERT_CHILD
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `00 00 00 00` A = parentId = 0
 - `01 00 00 00` B = childId = 1
 - `FF FF FF FF` C = APPEND (`u32::MAX`)
 
 ### 3. TREE:MOVE_CHILD (parent=1, child=2, newIndex=0)
 
 ```
 01 05 00 00 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
 ```
 
 - `01` category = TREE
 - `05` command = MOVE_CHILD
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `01 00 00 00` A = parentId = 1
 - `02 00 00 00` B = childId = 2
 - `00 00 00 00` C = newIndex = 0
 
 ### 4. STYLE:SET_PROPERTY (id=1, propertyId=SPACING=0x0001, valueType=F32, 4.0)
 
 ```
 02 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 01 00 04 00 00 00 80 40
 ```
 
 - `02` category = STYLE
 - `01` command = SET_PROPERTY
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `01 00 00 00` A = nodeId = 1
 - `01 00 04 00` B = `(valueType << 16) | propertyId` = `(0x04 << 16) | 0x0001`
   - low two bytes `01 00` = propertyId = 0x0001 (SPACING)
   - high byte `04` = valueType = 0x04 (F32)
 - `00 00 80 40` C = 4.0 (f32 LE: 0x40800000)
 
 ### 5. STYLE:SET_PROPERTY (id=1, propertyId=COLOR=0x100A, valueType=COLOR=0x07, rgba=0xFF0000FF)

 02 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 0A 10 07 00 FF 00 00 FF
 ```
 
 - `02` category = STYLE
 - `01` command = SET_PROPERTY
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `01 00 00 00` A = nodeId = 1
 - `0A 10 07 00` B = `(valueType << 16) | propertyId` = `(0x07 << 16) | 0x100A`
   - low two bytes `0A 10` = propertyId = 0x100A (COLOR)
   - high byte `07` = valueType = 0x07 (COLOR)

 ```

 ```
 
 - `02` category = STYLE
 - `03` command = SET_TEXT

 - `01 00 00 00` A = nodeId = 1
 - `00 00 00 00` B = arenaRef = 0 (entry is `[u32 length][bytes]` in the arena)
 - `00 00 00 00` C = 0

 ```

 - `01` command = RESET
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `00 00 00 00` A = 0
 - `00 00 00 00` B = 0
 - `00 00 00 00` C = 0

 - `03` category = EVENT
 - `01` command = POINTER_DOWN
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `05 00 00 00` A = targetId = 5
 - `00 00 20 41` B = 10.0 (f32 LE: 0x41200000)
 - `00 00 A0 41` C = 20.0 (f32 LE: 0x41A00000)
 
 ### 9. EVENT:POINTER_MOVE (target=5, x=10.0, y=20.0, hovering)
 
 ```
 03 02 01 00 05 00 00 00 00 00 20 41 00 00 A0 41
 ```
 
 - `03` category = EVENT
 - `02` command = POINTER_MOVE
 - `01 00` flags = 0x0001 (`HOVER_ENTER`)
 - `05 00 00 00` A = targetId = 5
 - `00 00 20 41` B = 10.0 (f32 LE: 0x41200000)
 - `00 00 A0 41` C = 20.0 (f32 LE: 0x41A00000)
 
 ### 10. EVENT:POINTER_UP (target=5, x=10.0, y=20.0)
 
 ```
 03 03 00 00 05 00 00 00 00 00 20 41 00 00 A0 41
 ```
 
 - `03` category = EVENT
 - `03` command = POINTER_UP
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `05 00 00 00` A = targetId = 5
 - `00 00 20 41` B = 10.0 (f32 LE: 0x41200000)
 - `00 00 A0 41` C = 20.0 (f32 LE: 0x41A00000)
 
 ### 11. EVENT:KEY_DOWN (target=5, keyCode='A'=0x41, modifiers=0x01, repeat)
 
 ```
 03 04 02 00 05 00 00 00 41 00 00 00 01 00 00 00
 ```
 
 - `03` category = EVENT
 - `04` command = KEY_DOWN
 - `02 00` flags = 0x0002 (`KEY_REPEAT`)
 - `05 00 00 00` A = targetId = 5
 - `41 00 00 00` B = keyCode = 0x41 (`'A'`, low u16)
 - `01 00 00 00` C = modifiers = 0x01 (low u8)
 
 ### 12. EVENT:KEY_UP (target=5, keyCode='A'=0x41, modifiers=0x01)
 
 ```
 03 05 00 00 05 00 00 00 41 00 00 00 01 00 00 00
 ```
 
 - `03` category = EVENT
 - `05` command = KEY_UP
 - `00 00` flags = 0
 - `05 00 00 00` A = targetId = 5
 - `41 00 00 00` B = keyCode = 0x41 (`'A'`, low u16)
 - `01 00 00 00` C = modifiers = 0x01 (low u8)

 ## Directions
 
 - `TREE` / `STYLE` are **guest → host** (application → renderer).
 - `EVENT` is **host → guest** (renderer → application): raw pointer/keyboard
   inputs with a host-resolved `targetId`. A conforming EVENT encoder/decoder
   MUST reproduce vectors 8–12 exactly.
 - `META` is both directions.
 
 ## Frame Conformance
 
 A complete frame is: delta opcodes written into consecutive ring slots, then a
 `frameCount` increment in the header block. Ring slot `i` occupies bytes
 `[ringOffset + i*16, ringOffset + i*16 + 16)`.
 
 The header block layout and ring semantics are defined in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#linear-memory-layout).
 
+The host → guest event ring shares the same 16-byte slot format and lives at
+`eventRingOffset` (header `0x2A`), with `eventReadCursor` (0x36, guest-owned)
+and `eventWriteCursor` (0x3A, host-owned). A host writing `EVENT:POINTER_UP`
+into the event ring must reproduce the exact vector-11 bytes in the slot at
+`eventWriteCursor`, then advance `eventWriteCursor`; the guest advances
+`eventReadCursor` after draining.
+
 ## Network Batch Conformance
 
 A network batch serializes opcodes + an arena delta (see
 [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#transport)). A conforming batch encoder/decoder MUST
 reproduce the following bytes exactly.
 
 ### 13. NETWORK:BATCH (frameCount=1, one CREATE_NODE, arena delta = "Hi")

 delta is the self-describing entry for `"Hi"`: `[02 00 00 00][48 69]`.

 4C 50 4C 50 01 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 01 00 00 00
 01 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
 06 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 48 69
 ```
 
 - `4C 50 4C 50` = magic `PLPL` (u32 `0x504C504C`, little-endian)
 - `01 00` = version 1
 - `00 00` = flags (guest → host)
 - `01 00 00 00` = frameCount = 1
 - `01 00 00 00` = opcodeCount = 1
 - `01 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` = the CREATE_NODE opcode (16 bytes)
 - `06 00 00 00` = arenaDeltaLen = 6
 - `02 00 00 00 48 69` = arena entry `[len=2]["Hi"]`
 
 ### 14. NETWORK:BATCH (frameCount=2, empty opcode list, empty arena delta)
 
 ```
 4C 50 4C 50 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
 00 00 00 00
 ```
 
 - `4C 50 4C 50` = magic `PLPL` (u32 `0x504C504C`, little-endian)
 - `01 00` = version 1
 - `00 00` = flags
 - `02 00 00 00` = frameCount = 2
 - `00 00 00 00` = opcodeCount = 0
 - `00 00 00 00` = arenaDeltaLen = 0
